explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, “I will sweep away man and beast; I will sweep away the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea, and the idols with their wicked worshipers.” (Zephaniah 1:3) The idols are named right there, and so are their wicked worshipers. So the statement is true. Good eye.

Close, friend, but the list keeps going. After man and beast, the birds and the fish, the LORD says, “…and the idols with their wicked worshipers.” (Zephaniah 1:3) So the idols are named right there in the verse. It's easy to stop reading once the animals show up.

Priests it is. The LORD says He will cut off “…every remnant of Baal, the names of the idolatrous and pagan priests…” (Zephaniah 1:4) Baal is a false god, and the verse lists the remnant of Baal and then the names of those priests. Priests is the word that fills the blank. Nice work, friend.

Soldiers would make a dramatic verse, friend, but that's not the word here. The verse says the LORD will cut off “…the names of the idolatrous and pagan priests…” (Zephaniah 1:4) I'm a stamper with a mustache, so I'd make a terrible soldier anyway. Priests is the one.

Builders, huh? I like the idea of a nice honest trade in there, friend, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says He will cut off “…the names of the idolatrous and pagan priests…” (Zephaniah 1:4) Priests, not builders, is the word that fits.

That's the one. The LORD describes those “…who bow down and swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom…” (Zephaniah 1:5) See that word "also"? These people swear by the LORD, but they swear by Milcom too. That's the problem right there.
Chemosh is a real name in the Bible, a false god of Moab (1 Kings 11:7). But it isn't the name in this verse. Zephaniah 1:5 says they “…also swear by Milcom…” Milcom is the answer here.
Dagon is a Bible name too, a god of the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:2). He isn't in this verse, though, friend. The LORD says they “…also swear by Milcom…” (Zephaniah 1:5) That's the name to hold onto.

Not quite, friend. The LORD describes them as “…those who turn back from following the LORD, neither seeking the LORD nor inquiring of Him.” (Zephaniah 1:6) So these people are doing neither one. The statement is false.

Right. The verse says they are “…those who turn back from following the LORD, neither seeking the LORD nor inquiring of Him.” (Zephaniah 1:6) That "neither, nor" shuts the door on both. Turning back means they aren't seeking and they aren't inquiring.

explanations.answer: The Day of the LORD is near
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The verse says, “Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near.” (Zephaniah 1:7) That "for" gives the reason. The nearness of that day is why the call goes out.

explanations.answer: The king of Judah has died
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse says a king has died, friend. The reason is right there in the text: “Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near.” (Zephaniah 1:7) That's the answer. Sometimes we make up a reason before reading the one on the page.

Closing doors would make a fine reason, but the verse doesn't say that. It says, “Be silent in the presence of the Lord GOD, for the Day of the LORD is near.” (Zephaniah 1:7) So the reason is the nearness of the Day of the LORD.

explanations.answer: The princes and the sons of the king
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says, “On the Day of the LORD’s sacrifice I will punish the princes, the sons of the king…” (Zephaniah 1:8) They're named first, before anyone else on the list. Sharp reading, friend.

Farmers and shepherds don't show up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “…I will punish the princes, the sons of the king…” (Zephaniah 1:8) Those are the first ones named. Check the order and you'll spot it.

explanations.answer: The soldiers at the city gates
explanations.explanation: Soldiers at the gates would sound dramatic, but the verse doesn't name them. The LORD says, “…I will punish the princes, the sons of the king…” (Zephaniah 1:8) Those are the first ones named, so that's your answer.

True, friend. The LORD says He will punish “…the princes, the sons of the king, and all who are dressed in foreign apparel.” (Zephaniah 1:8) After the princes and the sons of the king comes that next group. I looked down at my apron real quick, just to be safe.

Let's look again, friend. The LORD says, “…I will punish the princes, the sons of the king, and all who are dressed in foreign apparel.” (Zephaniah 1:8) So foreign apparel is right there in the verse. The statement is true.

Yes, friend. The LORD says He will punish “…all who leap over the threshold, who fill the house of their master with violence and deceit.” (Zephaniah 1:9) Those two words are what fills that house. The verse names both of them plainly. Well read.

Pride and boasting sound like they'd fit, but they aren't the words in the verse. The LORD says these people “…fill the house of their master with violence and deceit.” (Zephaniah 1:9) So violence and deceit are what's in that house.

Idols did come up earlier in this passage, so I see why that pulled at you. But verse 9 says these people “…fill the house of their master with violence and deceit.” (Zephaniah 1:9) Idols and incense aren't named here. Violence and deceit are.

Right, baker. The LORD says, “Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow, for all your merchants will be silenced; all who weigh out silver will be cut off.” (Zephaniah 1:11) The wailing comes with the silencing of the merchants. The verse also says all who weigh out silver will be cut off. Nice work.

explanations.answer: Their wells will all run dry
explanations.explanation: Wells running dry would be a sad sight, but the verse never mentions wells. The LORD says, “Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow, for all your merchants will be silenced…” (Zephaniah 1:11) The merchants being silenced is the reason for the wail.

explanations.answer: Their king will be taken away
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse is about a king being taken. The LORD says, “Wail, O dwellers of the Hollow, for all your merchants will be silenced; all who weigh out silver will be cut off.” (Zephaniah 1:11) The merchants are the ones in view.

explanations.answer: The LORD will do nothing either good or bad
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says He will punish “…the men settled in complacency, who say to themselves, ‘The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad.’” (Zephaniah 1:12) They figure He'll do nothing at all. Good reading, friend.

explanations.answer: The LORD will protect us no matter what
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a comfy thought, but it isn't what these men say. The verse has them saying, “The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad.” (Zephaniah 1:12) They're not counting on protection. They're counting on Him doing nothing.

explanations.answer: The LORD only judges the other nations
explanations.explanation: That's a believable thing for someone to say, but the text doesn't put it in their mouths. The men settled in complacency say to themselves, “The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad.” (Zephaniah 1:12) That's the line the verse gives.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “They will build houses but not inhabit them, and plant vineyards but never drink their wine.” (Zephaniah 1:13) They build the houses, but they won't live in them. So the statement is false.

Yes, it's false. The LORD says, “They will build houses but not inhabit them, and plant vineyards but never drink their wine.” (Zephaniah 1:13) The building happens, but the living there doesn't. Good catch, friend.

I get why it might sound that way, since mighty people usually look unshakable. But that's not what the text says. It says, “Then the cry of the mighty will be bitter.” (Zephaniah 1:14) The mighty are crying out, and the cry is bitter. So the statement is false.
Correct. Verse 14 says, “Then the cry of the mighty will be bitter.” (Zephaniah 1:14) A bitter cry doesn't sound like someone standing strong and unshaken. Even the mighty are crying out on that day.

explanations.answer: A day of darkness and gloom
explanations.explanation: That's on the list, friend. The LORD calls it “…a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness…” (Zephaniah 1:15) It's a heavy list, line after line. You read it right.

explanations.answer: A day of famine and drought
explanations.explanation: Famine and drought aren't on this list. The verse says, “…a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of destruction and desolation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness…” (Zephaniah 1:15) The match is darkness and gloom. It's a heavy list, so take your time with it.

explanations.answer: A day of plague and sickness
explanations.explanation: Plague and sickness aren't in this list. Verse 15 says, “…a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of destruction and desolation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness…” (Zephaniah 1:15) The match is darkness and gloom. It's a heavy passage, friend.

True. The LORD says that day is “…a day of horn blast and battle cry against the fortified cities, and against the high corner towers.” (Zephaniah 1:16) Even the cities built to be strong are named. Well done, friend.

Look again, friend. The verse says that day is “…a day of horn blast and battle cry against the fortified cities, and against the high corner towers.” (Zephaniah 1:16) The horn blast and battle cry are right there. So the statement is true.

Blind, friend, you nailed it. The LORD says, “I will bring such distress on mankind that they will walk like the blind…” (Zephaniah 1:17) Notice that little word "like." The verse gives a comparison for how people will walk, and the distress comes first.

Yes, sinned. The verse says they will walk like the blind “…because they have sinned against the LORD.” (Zephaniah 1:17) The text states the reason itself. First comes the walking like the blind, then the reason: sinned against the LORD. Nice reading.
Rich sounds like it could fit, friend, but it isn't the word in this verse. The LORD says people will walk like the blind. (Zephaniah 1:17) Blind is the one that fills the blank.

Spoken sounds like it could fit, friend, but it isn't the word the verse uses. The LORD says this happens “…because they have sinned against the LORD.” (Zephaniah 1:17) Sinned is the word in the blank.

Swear does show up earlier in this passage, where some “…swear by the LORD but also swear by Milcom…” (Zephaniah 1:5) But this blank wants a different word. Verse 17 says, “…because they have sinned against the LORD.” (Zephaniah 1:17)

That's it, friend. The LORD says, “Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the Day of the LORD’s wrath.” (Zephaniah 1:18) Silver and gold are the two the verse names, and neither one can deliver them on that day. That's the answer straight from the verse. Good reading.

Horses and chariots aren't in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the Day of the LORD’s wrath.” (Zephaniah 1:18) Silver and gold are the two named.

Allies in Egypt don't appear in this verse. The LORD says, “Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the Day of the LORD’s wrath.” (Zephaniah 1:18) So the answer is silver and gold. Keep your eyes on the text and you'll catch these.
